meta.title: Who really said "Tolerance and apathy are the last virtues of a dying society"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No. This line is a modern fabrication falsely pinned on Aristotle — it appears nowhere in his works and is unattested in antiquity, per Vassar’s Pharos and classicists.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Tolerance and apathy are the last virtues of a dying society'?
meta.ogDescription: A fake Aristotle quote. It appears in none of his works, is alien to ancient Greek thought, and traces to modern hard-right internet memes.

answer.label: Not Aristotle — a modern fabrication
answer.authorDates: No confirmed author · unattested before the 20th century
answer.sourceLine: Aristotle never wrote this. The line is absent from his entire surviving corpus and is alien to ancient Greek ideas — it uses “tolerance” and “dying society” in a distinctly modern sense. As Vassar’s Pharos project and the classicists at Sententiae Antiquae document, it is a recent slogan — its nearest documented ancestor is a hard-right/evangelical line (“Tolerance is the last virtue of a depraved society”) — retro-fitted onto Aristotle’s name to lend it authority.

source.heading: The source that doesn’t exist

docMeta.dd: Fabricated — not in any work of Aristotle

source.excerpt: Tolerance and apathy are the last virtues of a dying society.
trail: Pharos (Vassar College) catalogues this as a “Fake Aristotle Quote,” tracing its viral spread to a now-deplatformed Facebook page, “Smash Cultural Marxism — The Originals.”
The classicists at Sententiae Antiquae note the wording is alien to Aristotle and appears in “no books older than a decade or so,” mostly self-published texts.
WIST Quotations files it under Spurious: “Not found in the writings of Aristotle, or, with variation, anywhere earlier than the 19th Century.”

A related line — “Tolerance is the last virtue of a depraved society” — is instead linked to evangelical preacher D. James Kennedy and then to Hutton Gibson, per the classicists at Sententiae Antiquae; philosopher Gregory Sadler instead traces the “tolerance and apathy” line itself to James Kennedy.
source.excerptNote: Presented across social media as Aristotle’s words. No ancient Greek text — and no edition or translation of Aristotle — contains this sentence or anything close to it.

author.name: Aristotle
author.kicker: The philosopher who didn’t say it
author.heading: About Aristotle
author.metaLine: 384–322 BC · Greek philosopher · student of Plato, tutor of Alexander
author.bio: Aristotle of Stagira (384–322 BC) was a Greek philosopher whose surviving works — the Nicomachean Ethics, Politics, Rhetoric, Metaphysics and more — are among the most closely studied texts in the Western canon. Nothing resembling this sentence appears anywhere in that corpus. The concept of “tolerance” as a civic virtue and the framing of a “dying society” are modern; the line was pinned to his name centuries later to borrow his prestige.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most persistent fake Aristotle quotes — circulated as ancient wisdom but manufactured in modern times, often to give a veneer of classical authority to anti-immigrant and anti-multicultural politics.

items.why: The sentence is in none of Aristotle’s works and its vocabulary is anachronistic. WIST marks it spurious and unattested before the 19th century, and Sententiae Antiquae finds it in no book more than a decade or so old.

A related slogan — “Tolerance is the last virtue of a depraved society” — is linked to evangelical preacher D. James Kennedy and then to Hutton Gibson, per the classicists at Sententiae Antiquae. That is a modern political maxim, not Aristotle, and even it differs in wording from the “tolerance and apathy” meme — which Gregory Sadler traces to James Kennedy.
Pharos traces mass circulation to a now-deplatformed Facebook page, “Smash Cultural Marxism — The Originals,” while noting that page was neither the first nor the last to attach Aristotle’s name.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: Aristotle never said it. The line is a modern fabrication, unsupported by any text of his, as documented by Pharos and multiple classicists.

context.heading: Why this fake persists
lead: Fabricated quotes stick to Aristotle because his name is shorthand for reasoned authority. Attaching it to a slogan makes a contemporary opinion sound like a timeless law of history — which is precisely why fact-checkers at Vassar’s Pharos project flagged this one as a tool for lending “intellectual credibility” to xenophobic politics.

The tell is anachronism: Aristotle’s ethics prize virtues like courage, justice, and practical wisdom, and he had no concept of ‘tolerance’ as a modern civic value or of a ‘dying society’ in this rhetorical sense. When a line sounds like a 20th-century op-ed rather than a fourth-century-BC treatise, that is usually because it is.
context.pull: A line that sounds like an op-ed, not a treatise — because it is one.
